title: Applications of quantum annealing to magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants: First results beyond energies for atoms
authors: Boni Paul, Subimal Deb, Per Jönsson, Jörgen Ekman, Bhanu Pratap Das
abstract: We report the first results of the magnetic dipole hyperfine structure (HFS) constants of neutral $\mathrm{Li}$, Li-like $\mathrm{Be}$, neutral $\mathrm{Na}$, and Na-like $\mathrm{Mg}$ using a modified version of the Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm on D-Wave's quantum hardware. The results are benchmarked against relativistic configuration interaction with multiconfiguration Dirac Hartree-Fock (MCDHF) calculations using the General-purpose Relativistic Atomic Structure Package (GRASP), and simulated annealing. In our modified QAE, a zooming-and-sigma-annealing approach with a floating-point encoding scheme is adopted to estimate the ground-state eigenvalue and eigenvector of the relativistic Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian matrices ($H_{\mathrm{DC}}$) constructed from 11 or fewer configuration state functions (CSFs). For calculations with extended correlation orbital sets, we applied a CSF truncation scheme, retaining only CSFs (up to 12) that make significant contributions to the ground-state wavefunction. Our modified QAE precision is kept limited to three decimal places (up to 10 qubits). Hardware demonstrations on the D-Wave quantum processing unit (QPU) yielded results that were completely consistent with GRASP (at the chosen precision) in determining the magnetic dipole HFS constants, with accuracy varying across systems and $H_{\mathrm{DC}}$ matrix dimensions.
summary: The authors successfully applied a modified Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) algorithm on D-Wave hardware to calculate magnetic dipole hyperfine structure constants for several light atoms. By benchmarking these results against high-level classical calculations (GRASP), they demonstrated that quantum annealing can accurately determine complex atomic properties, marking an extension of the technique beyond ground-state energy determination.
main_problem: The primary goal is to calculate magnetic dipole hyperfine structure (HFS) constants for several light atoms using quantum annealing techniques, extending the application of these methods beyond simple ground-state energy calculations.
main_result: Quantum hardware demonstrations yielded HFS constant results completely consistent with established classical relativistic atomic structure calculations (GRASP) at the specified precision.
method: The problem is mapped onto a QUBO formulation suitable for quantum annealing, utilizing a modified Quantum Annealer Eigensolver (QAE) approach combined with a zooming-and-sigma-annealing technique.
model_or_system: The calculations focus on neutral and alkali-like atoms ($	ext{Li}, 	ext{Be}, 	ext{Na}, 	ext{Mg}$) using the relativistic Dirac-Coulomb Hamiltonian. The methodology involves constructing matrix elements from Configuration State Functions (CSFs).
key_observables: Magnetic dipole HFS constants ($A$) and ground-state eigenvalues/eigenvectors of the $	ext{HDC}$ matrix.
important_parameters: The QAE precision is limited to three decimal places, corresponding to up to 10 qubits; hardware constraints limit the number of CSFs used (e.g., $B=11$).
main_assumptions: A CSF truncation scheme is employed for larger basis sets, estimating contributions based on approximations derived from the independent electron pair model.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the iterative 'zooming' process used to improve eigenvalue precision during quantum annealing simulations.
paper_structure: The paper systematically presents comparisons of calculated CSF coefficients and HFS constants across multiple atomic species ($	ext{Li}, 	ext{Be}^+, 	ext{Na}, 	ext{Mg}^+$) using three methods: GRASP (reference), Simulated Annealing (SA), and Quantum Annealing (QA).
why_interesting: This work directly tests the capability of quantum annealers to solve complex, physically relevant many-body problems beyond simple energy minimization, providing a crucial benchmark for quantum simulation in atomic physics.
